No case tests pass-by-customization at all.

The 'technologies being used CAN achieve the visual presentation' gating clause: every case is a flat raster/SVG image; none probes whether the desired visual effect (font/spacing/anti-aliasing) was actually achievable in HTML/CSS — the threshold that distinguishes 1.4.5 (AA, with exception) from 1.4.9 (AAA, no exception) is never exercised.

The interaction-with-1.4.4 carve-out (Intent: 'using a technology to meet this criterion would interfere with meeting other criteria such as 1.4.4') — no case where text would break resize/reflow, so the image-justified-by-other-SC limb is absent.

Right-to-redistribute-font / not-widely-deployed-font justification as a PASS (Intent para 2): the Ivanhoe case is framed as a type sample, but no case passes specifically because the font is unavailable/unlicensed for live text.
The 'representation of a letter' / historical-document essential-presentation example (Understanding) — original-format-essential content is absent.

Genuine 'image of text used IN ADDITION TO equivalent text, both presented' PASS (Understanding 'event poster + text in CMS', para 5 note): the corpus has no positive case where an image of text is acceptable BECAUSE the same text is also provided as live text — the welcome.png case with adjacent text still FAILS.

Non-HTML/web technologies: PDF (technique PDF7, scanned-document OCR), and any non-web 'images of text'. EN C.9.1.4.5 covers ICT web pages but the OCR/PDF and document-format dimension is wholly missing.

Real-world image-of-text content TYPES from the SC examples are missing: styled headings rendered as bitmaps, navigation menus with image-of-text labels, a styled pull-quote as an image, multi-line paragraph text (only one paragraph-image case, textimage.jpg) — the 'styled headings / navigation items / a quote' examples in the Understanding doc.

The OCR-like detection difficulty (TT note: tester must first recognize an image CONTAINS text vs. being a photo/diagram): no borderline case (e.g., a diagram/screenshot/graph/infographic where text is incidental) to stress the detection vs. judgement split — graphs, screenshots, diagrams from the definition note are absent.
Anti-aliasing-on-all-user-agents justification (Intent) as a pass rationale — absent.
varietyGaps: ZERO ACT rules in scope and only ONE rule (0va7u6) backing all 15 cases — the entire corpus is a single rule's example set, so 'variety' is bounded by one rule's design, not the SC.

The pass/fail axis is almost entirely 'does the image's PIXELS contain readable words' (essentially an OCR + decorative-or-not test). The corpus does NOT exercise the SC's actual decision logic — essential vs. replaceable, customizable, can-the-tech-achieve-it — which is the part requiring human judgement and the part that distinguishes 1.4.5 from 1.4.9.

No customizable-controls case means the largest single SC limb (one of the two PASS conditions in TT Test 7.E) has 0% coverage — a tester/tool passing every corpus case could still completely miss customizable images of text.

Content domain is narrow: short English phrases/single words ('WCAG Rocks', 'Press me', 'Welcome to our website', resize 'A's) plus stock photos. No long-form text, no real UI chrome (headings, nav bars, menus, buttons-with-baked-in-labels at scale), no marketing/poster/infographic imagery, no multilingual or non-Latin script images of text.
No PDF / non-web technology cases despite PDF7 being a listed sufficient technique and EN framing it as ICT — pure HTML/CSS/SVG only.

Borderline/adversarial detection cases are missing: diagrams, screenshots, graphs, CAPTCHA (the definition-note exclusions and TT's named CAPTCHA exclusion) — the corpus never tests the hard 'is this text-in-a-picture or an image-of-text?' boundary.

The 'image of text PLUS equivalent live text = PASS' scenario (Understanding poster example, para-5 note) has no positive instance; the only paired-text case (welcome.png) is a FAIL, so the additive-text exception is represented only by its violation, never its satisfaction.

Failure modes are skewed to author MISTAKES (a div with no closing/self-closed, a data=/date= typo, alt='' on a meaningful image) rather than legitimate-but-wrong design decisions, so the corpus tests parser/markup edge cases more than genuine images-of-text policy violations.

aspects.title: False logotype / branding exemption — informational text dressed up as a brand mark
aspects.description: TT step 1a and the Understanding 'A logo containing text' example exempt logotypes ('text that is part of a logo or brand name') from 1.4.5 because 'the visual presentation of the text is essential to the identity of the logo.' The genuinely hard, human-only judgment is distinguishing a real wordmark/brand identity from ordinary informational text (a tagline, marketing slogan, navigation label, deadline notice, or paragraph of prose) that an author has merely set in a nice typeface, exported as an image, and parked in a header or wrapped in class='logo' to dodge the SC. A one-word company wordmark is exempt; 'Free shipping on orders over $50', 'Apply for your permit before March 31', or a styled <h1> baked into a banner is NOT a logotype even when it sits in a branding zone. A checker cannot OCR the text and reason about whether it functions as a brand identity vs. conveys substantive information; only a human can.
aspects.scLimb: Logotype / branding essential-presentation exception (Intent para 2; TT step 1a)
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus holds exactly one logo case (W3C logo as role=img CSS background = PASS) and one plain-text-image FAIL (textimage.jpg) at opposite extremes. There is no borderline where an image's text is ambiguous between 'brand identity' and 'ordinary informational text styled nicely' — the exact distinction TT step 1a turns on. The corpus never puts non-logo content into a branding context.

references.quote: Logotypes (text that is part of a logo or brand name) cannot be replaced by text.

The logo contains logotype (text as part, or all, of the logo). The visual presentation of the text is essential to the identity of the logo and is included as a gif image which does not allow the text characteristics to be changed.
This includes instances where a particular presentation of text is essential to the information being conveyed, such as type samples, logotypes, branding, etc.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build single self-contained HTML pages with images of text in a header/branding zone. For PASS pages, the image text is a genuine one-/two-word wordmark or crest. For FAIL pages, dress substantive informational text (tagline, slogan, deadline, navigation labels, a styled heading) in the same branding treatment — often with alt text equal to the visible text so a captioned-image heuristic would be fooled. Pair visually-similar PASS/FAIL twins so the verdict hinges purely on the semantic logotype-vs-information judgment, not on visual presentation.
suggestedScenarios: Header with a genuine one-word company wordmark image (alt='Acme', exempt) directly above a SECOND banner image baking in the full marketing tagline 'Acme — the smartest way to manage your money, every day' (ordinary text, FAIL) — same visual zone, opposite verdicts.
A custom-typeface brand-name logo (legitimately exempt) vs. the identical typographic treatment applied to the page's section heading 'Our 2026 Pricing Plans' rendered as an image with class='logo'.

A navigation bar where each item ('Home', 'Products', 'About', 'Contact') is a separate image of text styled to look uniformly branded; argued as 'part of the brand look' but they are navigation labels (Understanding 'Navigation items') that must be live text.

A government department crest (image, exempt logo) beside a sub-banner image reading 'Apply for your permit before March 31' — the crest passes, the deadline notice is informational image-of-text that fails.

A promotional badge image whose visible text is a slogan with substantive information ('Free shipping on orders over $50'), alt='Free shipping on orders over $50' supplied — a captioned image to a tool, but non-brand promotional text that should be selectable/resizable live text.
A footer 'logo wall' of partner-company wordmarks (each exempt) vs. one tile in the same wall that is actually a sentence of legal disclaimer text styled to match the logos (FAIL).

aspects.title: Customizability exception — image of text adjustable (or fake-adjustable) via on-page controls (C30)
aspects.description: The SC text itself passes images of text 'where a particular presentation of text is essential or can be visually customized,' and TT Test 7.E condition 2 passes an image of text if it 'can be visually customized: adjust the font, size, color, and background with controls provided by the web page.' Technique C30 (CSS image-replacement with a switch control) and the Understanding 'Dynamically Generated Images' / 'Customizable font settings' examples are the canonical PASS-by-customization route. Evaluating this requires a human to find the controls, operate them, and judge whether activating them actually swaps the image for live text or genuinely re-renders the image to the user's font/size/color — and crucially to catch the FAILURE where controls are present but FAKE (decorative, broken, or only change unrelated styling). A static checker sees pixels and DOM, not whether a button truly re-renders an image of text; this is human-operable judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Customizable-presentation exception (SC clause 'can be visually customized'; TT Test 7.E condition 2; technique C30)
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT case is a static flat raster/SVG image with no UI controls at all; the customizability limb of the SC is entirely unexercised in either direction. The corpus has no C30 switch and no dynamically-generated image, so neither a genuine PASS-by-customization nor a fake-controls FAIL is represented.

references.quote: Determine if the image of text can be visually customized: adjust the font, size, color, and background with controls provided by the web page.
Images of text can also be used where it is possible for users to customize the image of text to match their requirements.
Check that when the control is activated the resulting page includes text (programmatically determined text) wherever images of text had been used.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages that render a heading/body as an image of text alongside visible controls (A- A A+, colour toggle, 'View as plain text' link). For PASS pages, wire the control with client-side script so it truly swaps the image for live text or re-renders the image at the chosen size/colour. For FAIL pages, present the same control UI but make it inert/decorative, or make it change only unrelated page styling while the image-of-text bitmap stays fixed. A human must operate each control to decide. Keep all script inline so each page is self-contained.
suggestedScenarios: Heading rendered as an image of text PLUS a working 'A- A A+' / colour-toggle that actually re-renders the image at the chosen size and colour (genuine C30 PASS) — confirmed only by operating the control.
Deceptive twin: identical layout and same 'A- A A+' buttons, but they are decorative <span>s with no handler, so the image of text never changes (FAIL despite visible controls a tool would 'see').

A 'View as plain text' link near the top of the page (per C30) that swaps an image-of-text logo-heading for live <h1> text on click; verify the switched view truly provides programmatically-determined text wherever images had been.
A 'customize' control that changes only the surrounding page background colour while the image-of-text body remains a fixed bitmap — superficially customizable, substantively not (FAIL).

A dynamically generated quote image with a font/size selector that re-requests the image (?size=...): the control works but enlarging produces blurry pixelated text — borderline FAIL on the no-pixelation sub-requirement (TT note 2a).

A working size/colour control that DOES re-render, but the re-rendered image still omits part of the original text — controls present and functional yet the customized output is not equivalent (FAIL).

aspects.title: 'Significant other visual content' exclusion — graphs, screenshots, diagrams, infographics vs. text-only images
aspects.description: The images-of-text definition note excludes 'text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content,' citing 'graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text' (TT adds CAPTCHA). The detection step is explicitly OCR-like: the tester must FIRST decide whether an image that contains text is fundamentally a graph/screenshot/diagram/infographic (out of scope, INAPPLICABLE) or is an image-of-text dressed up (in scope, potentially FAIL). This is the most subjective limb of the SC: a human must weigh whether the non-text graphics are 'significant' enough to exclude the image, or whether it is predominantly text laid out decoratively. No automated checker can make this gestalt judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Definition exclusion: pictures with significant other visual content are not 'images of text'
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT's INAPPLICABLE/PASS pictures contain no text at all (fireworks, Times Square, books — clear non-applicability) and its FAIL images are essentially pure text on a plain field (clear applicability). The genuinely hard middle — an image that is largely text but also carries chart geometry, UI chrome, or diagram structure — is absent. No case forces the 'does the non-text visual content make this NOT an image of text?' judgment.

references.quote: This does not include text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content. Examples of such pictures include graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text.

EXCLUDE text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content such as CAPTCHA, graphs, screenshots, and diagrams, which visually convey important information more than just text.
the tester must first recognize that an image contains text (vs being a photo/diagram), then judge whether that text is essential (logotype) or could have been live text.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build PASS/INAPPLICABLE pages whose image carries genuine graphical encoding (bar geometry, screenshot chrome, boxes-and-arrows) where words are mere labels, and matching FAIL pages where the image LOOKS chart/diagram-like but is actually just styled text with no real graphical information (a 'chart' that is a text table, a 'flowchart' that is stacked sentences). Make the borderline tight so the verdict depends on judging whether the visual content is 'significant', not on whether text is present. Render charts/screenshots as static images embedded in self-contained HTML.
suggestedScenarios: A bar chart image with axis labels, legend and data values where the bar geometry carries the information (excluded 'graph', INAPPLICABLE) vs. a 'chart' image that is really a styled text table with no graphical encoding (in-scope image of text, FAIL).

A product screenshot of a software UI with menus and a dialog box (excluded 'screenshot') vs. an image cropped to nothing but a paragraph of release-notes text from that screenshot (effectively an image of text, FAIL).
An annotated flowchart where boxes-and-arrows carry meaning and words are labels (excluded 'diagram') vs. a 'flowchart' that is five sentences stacked with no boxes (in-scope image of text).
An infographic combining icons, a timeline graphic and several captions — human must decide whether graphic content is 'significant' or it is predominantly decoratively-laid-out text (FAIL).

A pricing comparison delivered as one image: visually a table grid with checkmark icons (graphic) but the cells are all numbers/words — borderline 'diagram with significant visual content' vs. an image of text that should be a live table.
A CAPTCHA image (distorted text on noise, explicitly excluded by TT) vs. a near-identical image that is clean stylized text masquerading as needing image form (in-scope, FAIL).

aspects.title: 'In addition to' MET condition — image of text accompanied by the same content as visible live text
aspects.description: The Understanding note: the SC 'is intended to address situations where images of text are used rather than text. Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.' The 'event poster + CMS text' example is the canonical PASS: the poster image would fail alone, but because the SAME text is ALSO posted as live, visible text next to it, 1.4.5 is satisfied. The hard human judgment is verifying EQUIVALENCE (same information, not a partial summary) AND VISIBILITY (genuinely presented to the user — not an alt attribute, not display:none, not sr-only, not stale content). A checker cannot judge semantic equivalence between an image's pixels and nearby live text, nor that both are 'presented.'
aspects.scLimb: 'In addition to text' met-condition (Understanding para 5 note; distinguishes 1.4.5 from 1.4.9)
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT's decorative-image-plus-text pair (welcome.png with adjacent text) still FAILS, so the corpus never demonstrates the SC being MET because equivalent live text is present in addition to the image. There is no positive 'in addition to' PASS, and no case probing whether the accompanying text is genuinely equivalent and presented vs. only partial/hidden.

references.quote: Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.

in addition to the image, they can add regular text to the calendar entry, so they post both the poster and the text contained in the image. This text is shown next to the poster image on the site's calendar page.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages pairing an image of text with nearby live text. PASS pages reproduce the FULL image text verbatim as visible live text adjacent to the image. FAIL pages break either equivalence (live text gives only a partial/summary/stale version) or visibility (the equivalent live text is display:none / sr-only / positioned offscreen so it is not 'presented to the user'). The judgment hinges on comparing image content to live text content and confirming both are visibly rendered.
suggestedScenarios: Event-poster image-of-text with the FULL poster text (date, venue, line-up, price) reproduced verbatim as visible live text directly beneath it — a genuine 'in addition to' PASS the corpus lacks.

Partial-equivalence FAIL: poster image-of-text whose accompanying live text gives only the event title but omits the date/venue/price present only in the image — 'in addition to' but not 'the same information'.

A promotional banner image reading 'Sale ends Friday — 30% off' with the same sentence as a live

nearby (MET) vs. a twin whose live text says merely 'Sale on now' (not equivalent, FAIL).

An image-of-text quotation card whose quote is ALSO a live <blockquote> with identical wording (MET) vs. one where the live blockquote is display:none / sr-only so it is NOT 'presented to the user' (note requires BOTH presented, FAIL).

A specials board photographed as an image with the day's specials typed as a visible live list below: wording matches exactly (PASS) vs. the live list being last week's stale specials (not the same information, FAIL).
An image of text whose only 'equivalent' is the alt attribute (no on-screen live text at all) — alt is not text 'presented to the user' in this sense, so the met-condition does not apply (FAIL).

aspects.title: Essential-presentation exceptions beyond logos — type samples, font-family specimens, historical documents, symbolic glyphs
aspects.description: Intent para 2 and the Understanding enumerate PASS-by-essential-presentation cases distinct from logotypes: a 'Representation of a font family' (substituting another font 'would defeat the purpose of the representation'), 'A representation of a letter' (an original historical document whose original format is essential to information about its time period), 'Symbolic text characters' (B/I/ABC editor buttons whose glyphs 'do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language'), and type samples. Judging these requires understanding WHY the presentation is essential — re-typesetting as live text would destroy the very thing communicated — and rejecting ABUSE where ordinary informational text is wrongly justified as 'a type sample' or 'historical look.' A checker cannot reason about whether a particular visual presentation is essential to meaning.
aspects.scLimb: Essential-presentation exception (non-logo branches): font specimen, historical original format, symbolic non-language glyphs
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus has the comic-cover type-sample (Ivanhoe) and maps the A/A resize buttons to symbolic characters, but never tests the historical/original-format-essential rationale, the symbolic-vs-human-language editor-glyph distinction in either direction, nor the abuse case where ordinary informational text is wrongly justified under the type-sample/font-representation exception. 'Essential' is asserted by the corpus rather than stress-tested.

references.quote: A web page contains a representation of an original letter. The depiction of the letter in its original format is essential to information being conveyed about the time period in which it was written.
A web page contains information about a particular font family. Substituting the font family with another font would defeat the purpose of the representation.

Some of the buttons use text characters that do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language. For example "B" to increase font weight, "I" to italicize the text and "ABC" to check the spelling.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build PASS/FAIL twins for each essential-presentation branch. PASS pages use images where the visual form is genuinely the point (a font specimen demonstrating letterforms, a scanned historical document, single symbolic non-language glyph buttons). FAIL pages apply the same surface justification to ordinary informational text (an article ABOUT a font whose own paragraphs are baked in that font; a modern retypeset masquerading as 'antique'; word-label buttons 'Bold'/'Italic' that ARE human language). Each judgment turns on whether re-typesetting would destroy essential meaning.
suggestedScenarios: A typography page showing a 'Garamond' specimen image laid out as 'The quick brown fox' to demonstrate letterforms (font-representation, PASS) vs. an article ABOUT Garamond whose own body paragraphs are baked into images set in Garamond (not a specimen, FAIL).

A history article showing a scanned 18th-century handwritten letter with a descriptive alt (original format essential, PASS) vs. the same article's body text presented as a scanned image 'to look antique' (no essential rationale, FAIL).

A rich-text editor toolbar of single symbolic glyph images 'B', 'I', 'ABC' with text alternatives (Understanding symbolic-characters PASS) vs. a toolbar whose buttons are full word-labels 'Bold', 'Italic', 'Spell check' rendered as images (human-language text, should be live, FAIL).

A museum page presenting a constitution facsimile where the original calligraphy is the point (PASS) vs. a 'reproduction' that merely retypesets the document's words in a modern font and saves as PNG (FAIL).

A page wrapping an ordinary multi-paragraph terms-of-service in an image and labelling it 'type sample' to claim the exception — a human must reject the bogus essential-presentation justification (FAIL).
A mathematical/notation specimen image where the exact rendered glyph form is essential (PASS) vs. a plain prose sentence rendered as an image and called a 'specimen' (FAIL).

aspects.title: Core image-of-text-vs-live-text detection across delivery mechanisms and decoy live text
aspects.description: The SC's foundational requirement — 'If the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, text is used to convey information rather than images of text' — depends on a human first recognizing that an image actually contains rendered text (OCR-like detection) and then confirming the same visual effect was achievable in HTML/CSS so the content should have been live text. The hard cases require semantic judgment: text baked into a CSS background-image or pseudo-element (no , no alt, invisible to most checkers), text rendered via SVG inside an image vs. live selectable SVG , web-font glyph text that looks like an image but is real text, and decoys where author-supplied alt or a hidden sr-only string makes a tool believe live text exists when the displayed content is still a bitmap. No automated tool reliably OCRs arbitrary images and judges achievability; this is core human semantic/visual work.
aspects.scLimb: Core SC requirement: live text rather than images of text where the visual presentation is technologically achievable
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT exercises multiple embedding technologies but only at clear extremes (pure-text image FAIL vs. text-free photo PASS, plus one live-SVG-text INAPPLICABLE). It never tests the achievability gating clause (whether the desired visual effect was actually attainable in HTML/CSS), nor the deceptive middle where text is hidden in CSS backgrounds/pseudo-elements or where decoy live text/alt masks a bitmap. The threshold distinguishing achievable-so-must-be-live from genuinely-not-achievable is unexercised.

references.quote: Determine if text can be used instead of the image of text to present the same effect and information.
If authors can use text to achieve the same visual effect, they should present the information as text rather than using an image.
Rather than using bitmap images to present headings in a specific font and size, an author uses CSS to achieve the same result.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages that hide image-of-text in non-obvious delivery paths and add decoys. FAIL pages: a heading or pull-quote whose text is a CSS background-image or ::before content with no /alt; a styled menu where labels are background-image sprites; a paragraph baked into an inline SVG . PASS/INAPPLICABLE foils: the visually identical effect achieved with live HTML+CSS (web font, letter-spacing), or genuinely live selectable SVG . Add decoy alt strings or sr-only text that name the content while the displayed pixels remain a bitmap. The judgment turns on detecting hidden image-text and on whether CSS could have achieved the look.
suggestedScenarios:
A site heading whose text is a CSS background-image (no , no alt) styled to look like an ordinary

— invisible to alt-based checkers, but an image of text whose effect is trivially achievable in CSS (FAIL) vs. a twin

using a web font (live text, PASS).
A styled pull-quote rendered as a single PNG of text vs. the identical-looking quote built with live HTML + CSS (italic, indent, web font) per the Understanding 'A quote' example.
A navigation menu where each label is a CSS background-image sprite of styled text (FAIL) vs. the same menu with live text labels and CSS styling (PASS).

An image showing a multi-line paragraph of body prose set in a special font where that exact look IS achievable with @font-face (FAIL) — contrast a single decorative ornamental drop-cap glyph where the form is arguably essential.
A bitmap heading whose alt attribute repeats the heading text (a tool sees 'text present') yet the rendered content is still a non-resizable image (FAIL) — decoy alt does not satisfy 1.4.5.

Live, selectable SVG <text> rendered inline (real text, INAPPLICABLE/PASS) vs. an SVG that rasterizes the same words into an <image> bitmap (image of text, FAIL) — visually indistinguishable, opposite verdicts.

pages.scenario: Fintech masthead 'brand lockup': a genuine one-word wordmark image ('Northwind', exempt logotype) stacked directly above a second image whose pixels spell the full marketing tagline 'Northwind — the smartest way to manage your money, every day', styled to read as part of the logo. Same branding zone, opposite verdicts; the tagline is ordinary marketing prose that must be live text.
pages.mechanism: The tagline's words are SVG <text> glyphs in an inline-SVG data: URI (verified: string absent from document.body.innerText; rasterises at 200% zoom). A low-vision user cannot resize/recolour the sentence because it is pixels, not text. The wordmark image shares that limitation but is PERMITTED under the logotype exemption; the tagline is NOT, because the same information is expressible as styled live text with the author's technologies, so text must be used (1.4.5).
pages.primarySelector: header.masthead img.tagline-banner[alt="Northwind — the smartest way to manage your money, every day"]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both have non-empty, accurate alt, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse image-alt passes for both and there is no missing-attribute defect. No tool OCRs the pixels, and none can reason that the 'Northwind' image is a brand identity (exempt) while the identically-styled tagline image is a marketing sentence (not exempt). The pass/fail split is a pure logotype-vs-ordinary-text semantic judgment.

citation.quote: The logo contains logotype (text as part, or all, of the logo). The visual presentation of the text is essential to the identity of the logo and is included as a gif image which does not allow the text characteristics to be changed.

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page where the real brand name 'Quanta' is live text, but the pricing section's heading 'Our 2026 Pricing Plans' is rendered as a flat image and wrapped in <div class="logo" role="img" aria-label="Our 2026 Pricing Plans">, set in the brand display face, argued to be 'branding'. A styled section heading is WCAG's canonical image-of-text example, not a logo.
pages.mechanism: The heading exists only as SVG glyphs inside an wrapped by role="img". The role=img has an accessible name via aria-label so a screen reader hears the words, but 1.4.5 concerns visual customisation: a low-vision user who needs the title at 200% in their own colours gets a blurred raster instead of reflowed, recoloured text. citation.quote: Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.

pages.scenario: Interior-architecture studio testimonial: a designed quote-card image of text, paired in the DOM with a live <blockquote> containing word-for-word identical wording 'in addition to' the image — but the <blockquote> carries the studio's reusable visually-hidden (sr-only 1px clip-path:inset(50%)) helper, so it is removed from the visible page. Equivalence is perfect; visibility is broken.
pages.mechanism: A screen-reader user does hear the full quote from the clipped <blockquote>, but 1.4.5 protects people who can SEE text yet need to restyle it. For a low-vision user who needs the quote at 200% in high contrast, the only thing on screen is the immutable image; the equivalent text is clipped to a 1px offscreen box and cannot be enlarged, recoloured, or reflowed. The note requires BOTH the image and the text be 'presented to the user'; hidden text is exposed to AT but not visibly presented, so the met-condition does not apply.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: visually-hidden/sr-only text is an intentional, ubiquitous pattern; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse treat clipped-but-present text as fine (it is in the a11y tree, has no contrast problem because it isn't painted), and image-alt passes. No tool reasons that, specifically for 1.4.5, the equivalent text must be VISIBLY presented so a low-vision user can restyle it, not merely reachable by a screen reader. Distinguishing 'exposed to AT' from 'presented to the user' for this SC is human judgment about who 1.4.5 protects.

citation.quote: Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met. This allows authors to convey content using any styling they desire, while also presenting the information in text, which can then be manipulated by users to make it more distinguishable.

pages.scenario: Café daily-specials: a photographed chalkboard image of text shows TODAY's specials (Spiced Parsnip Soup £6.50 / Wild Mushroom Risotto £12.50 / Sticky Toffee Pudding £6.00); the live 'Text version' <ul> beneath it was not refreshed this week and still lists LAST week's specials and prices (Carrot & Coriander Soup £6.00 / Beef Lasagne £11.95 / Lemon Cheesecake £5.50). Both are presented, but they convey different menus.
pages.mechanism: A sighted customer reads today's specials off the photo; a blind or low-vision user relying on the restyleable text version hears last week's stale menu and wrong prices — actively misleading. The 'in addition to' met-condition requires the accompanying text to convey the SAME information as the image; stale text conveys DIFFERENT information, so the condition is not satisfied and 1.4.5 is not met.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Nothing is malformed: the board photo has a sensible alt, the <ul> is valid and high-contrast, image-alt passes. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not OCR the chalkboard, do not parse the live list, and have no notion of which version is current. Detecting that the two disagree — and that the text is the stale one — requires a human to read both and apply freshness/equivalence judgment.

citation.quote: Determine if text can be used instead of the image of text to present the **same effect and information**.

pages.scenario: District-council garden-waste notice: the entire substantive notice (collection day change, £45 subscription, 20 June deadline, 'will not be emptied' warning, renewal URL/phone) is a single image of text with a faithful, complete alt attribute; there is NO visible live-text version of the notice anywhere on the page. The image of text is used instead of text, with a text alternative bolted on — not in addition to visible text.

But 1.4.5 protects users who can SEE text yet need to change how it looks; for them the alt is invisible — exposed only to AT, never rendered, so it cannot be enlarged, recoloured, or reflowed on screen. The 'in addition to text' met-condition specifically requires text 'presented to the user' (visible live text alongside the image); an alt attribute is not that, so the condition does not apply and the image of text fails 1.4.5.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has a long, accurate alt, so image-alt passes and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse treat it as a model image. None OCRs the graphic to discover its pixels ARE the notice (text that could trivially be HTML), and none has any concept of the 1.4.5 distinction between 'alt present' and 'visible live text present in addition.' Recognising the whole notice is a picture, and reasoning that a text alternative is not text 'presented to the user,' is human visual + semantic judgment.

pages.scenario: Residential-building water-shutoff notice: a single bilingual flyer image of text contains both an ENGLISH block and an ESPAÑOL block carrying the same shutoff details; the resident portal renders a live 'Text version' 'in addition to' the image, but a volunteer transcribed only the English half. A Spanish-reading resident who is blind, or who has low vision and needs to enlarge/recolour, gets their language only as immutable image pixels (the image alt is just a label) — for them the image of text is used instead of text.
